solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A small row after noon is more unpleasant

indicators.note: one thing coming after another sets the order in which the pieces are joined

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for noon
taken as written
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a tier is a row, as of seats in a theatre

explanation.surface: A minor quarrel breaking out in the afternoon makes things even more unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' tempts as a quarrel, but it is a line of seats; the whole string sits after the noon abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nastier is worse or more disagreeable; the comparative forms match exactly.

clue.text: So-so description of low-seismic activity?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: mediocre, not very good
second meaning, read literally: an earthquake with only minor tremors

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical literal reading: a quake that produced only small tremors has no big shakes at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something mediocre or unimpressive, which is exactly what so-so means in casual speech.

clue.text: Bands get naked with soprano taking ecstasy

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so the pair of pieces admits another inside them

parts.note: to strip is to take off your clothes
S is the abbreviation for soprano
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A rock band strips off onstage while their singer takes drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bands' suggests musicians, but it means stripes of colour; the drug slips in between the undressing and the singer's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Stripes are long narrow strips of colour, which is one meaning of bands, both plural nouns.

clue.text: I figure on leaving one Latin country

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: when something leaves it is no longer there, so a letter departs from the word

parts.note: a tally is a count or total, a figure
L is the abbreviation for Latin; only one of the two in the figure goes

explanation.surface: Someone reckons that, leaving one Latin-speaking land, they will arrive in another.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so I sits on top. The figure has two L's and only one leaves, which is why the clue says 'one Latin'.
explanation.definitionFit: Italy is a nation in southern Europe, an example of a country, with Latin its historic language.

clue.text: Retsina I sent flying gets you most wet

indicators.note: things sent flying land scattered in disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written; retsina is a Greek resinated wine
taken as written

explanation.surface: I knocked over a glass of Greek wine and got drenched.
explanation.walkthrough: The spilt wine explains the wetness in the surface, but the wine and the pronoun are only letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Rainiest describes weather with the greatest rainfall, the superlative of wet in a climatic sense.

clue.text: State to arrest king? I don't believe it!

indicators.note: to arrest someone is to hold them captive, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: 'No way!' is an exclamation of disbelief
R is the abbreviation for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A government moving to arrest its own king prompts astonished disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a verb meaning to declare, but it is the noun for a nation. The king's letter lands between the two words of the exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Norway is a Scandinavian kingdom, one example of a sovereign nation or state.

clue.text: Song 2?
Erring ABC somehow preparing to have another hit?

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters come out arranged in some other way

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An American TV network that keeps getting things wrong is plotting its next hit show.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'hit' a success on the network; the definition means bracing yourself again for another blow.
explanation.definitionFit: To brace oneself is to steel against an impact, so doing it again readies you for a further blow.

clue.text: A brooding comic

parts.note: taken as written
musing is thinking deeply, brooding

explanation.surface: A moody, introspective stand-up comedian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comic' looks like a noun for a comedian, but here it is the adjective meaning funny.
explanation.definitionFit: Something amusing makes people laugh, which is the adjectival sense of comic.

clue.text: Matter primarily used in plant to make an element

indicators.note: something used in a thing is put inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: the geranium is a common flowering plant

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Some substance is fed into a factory plant to produce a chemical element.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as a factory in the surface, but it is a flower; one extra letter turns the flower into the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Germanium is a chemical element, a grey metalloid used in semiconductors, number 32 on the periodic table.

clue.text: Blunt lover describes foremost of letdowns

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: a buff is an enthusiast or lover of something, as in a film buff

indicators.note: foremost means the very front, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A frank partner describes the chief of their disappointments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describes' seems to mean tells about, but in geometry it means draws a line around.
explanation.definitionFit: A bluff manner is plain-spoken and hearty, which matches blunt as an adjective for frank, direct speech.

clue.text: Flatly mundane rubbish essentially

indicators.note: rubbish is junk, so the letters are treated as scrap to be broken up and remade

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict: something is, at heart, dull and worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish' looks like a verdict on the mundane thing, but it signals the rearrangement; every letter of the first two words is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adverbs mean at the most basic level, in the core nature of something.

clue.text: Vacuous politician toys with cuts regularly

parts.note: the blogged parse; the usual abbreviation for a Member of the European Parliament is MEP, so these letters look like a slip

indicators.note: cutting at regular intervals removes every other letter, leaving alternate ones behind

parts.note: the first and third letters of the word

explanation.surface: An empty-headed politician plays about with budget cuts on a regular basis.
explanation.walkthrough: The expected European politician is MEP; the letters needed are the same three in another order, which solvers have flagged as a flaw rather than a device.
explanation.definitionFit: Vacuous and empty both describe something lacking content or intelligence, as in an empty remark.

clue.text: Energy in sex helping repeated performance

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is placed within the rest

parts.note: IT is slang for sex or sex appeal
E is the symbol for energy in physics
a ration is a portion or helping of food

explanation.surface: Lively lovemaking earns an encore.
explanation.walkthrough: IT as sex comes from old slang, as in the 'It girl'. The energy letter goes into the pair made by the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: An iteration is a repetition of a process or act, a doing-again of the same thing.

clue.text: What can decide court battles in match around Kent

parts.note: a Test is an international cricket match
CA is short for circa, Latin for around
Kent is a county in the south-east of England

explanation.surface: Tennis battles on court, fought in a match somewhere near Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like it wants to put one piece round another, but here it simply gives the dating abbreviation. Kent is a county in England's south-east corner.
explanation.definitionFit: A test case is a lawsuit whose ruling sets a precedent for similar legal disputes that follow.

clue.text: Delighted to pawn a cage for Spooner?

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the start sounds trade places

parts.note: to hock something is to pawn it; its opening sound swaps with the cage's
taken as written
a coop is a cage for poultry; it takes the opening sound of the pawning word

explanation.surface: Someone is thrilled to pledge a birdcage at the pawnshop.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening H and C sounds of the two words turns them into the exultant idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means extremely pleased and exultant, a colourful way of saying overjoyed.

clue.text: It enables chap to get up though 50% of grates

definitions.text: It enables chap to get up

parts.note: a misprint for 'through': via means by way of, through

indicators.note: fifty per cent is half, so only half the letters of the word are kept

parts.note: the first half of the word

explanation.surface: Something helps a man climb up through the fireplace grates.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'though' is a typo for 'through', which is what gives the Latin-derived preposition. 'Get up' is a double entendre.
explanation.definitionFit: The branded drug treats erectile dysfunction, so it helps a man achieve an erection, the saucy sense of getting up.

clue.text: Ship's doctor catching last of lancet fish

parts.note: surface padding: it sets the scene of a ship's medic and gives no letters

indicators.note: catching something means holding on to it, so one piece takes in another

parts.note: a surgeon is a medical doctor who operates

indicators.note: the last of anything is its end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A ship's medic hooks a fish with the tip of a scalpel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ship's doctor' reads as one phrase, but the 's is only possessive surface; the doctor alone gives the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: The sturgeon is a large fish, the source of caviar.

clue.text: Hip Antifa leader brought under suspicion

indicators.note: bringing something under a thing puts it beneath its cover, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a hunch is a suspicion or intuition

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A trendy anti-fascist ringleader comes under police suspicion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hip' tempts as trendy, describing the activist, but it is the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: The haunch is the hip and upper thigh of a person or animal, so the two nouns name the same body area.

clue.text: Endure a Parisian leftist turning on Beat It

parts.note: un is French for 'a'

indicators.note: something turning faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a red is a left-wing radical
'beat it!' means go away

explanation.surface: A French left-winger puts up with a Michael Jackson record being played.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the first part above the last. 'Beat It' looks like the song title, but it is the command to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: To undergo is to experience or be subjected to something unpleasant, which is what enduring means.

clue.text: Do nothing in government about a failing Britain ultimately

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes around the others

parts.note: the state is the government of a country
taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so the final letters of the words are kept

parts.note: the final letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A political complaint: the government sits idle while Britain declines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Failing' looks like part of the picture of decline, but it only supplies its last letter alongside the other word's.
explanation.definitionFit: To stagnate is to stay inactive and make no progress, the verb sense of doing nothing.

clue.text: Books into a hotel by seedy soldiers' home?

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so one piece is put inside another

parts.note: taken as written
NT is the New Testament, the books of the Bible's second part
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
seedy can mean unwell, as in feeling seedy

explanation.surface: Someone checks into a run-down hotel near an army barracks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Books into' reads as checking in, but it puts the New Testament between the article and the hotel letter; 'seedy' means poorly, not shabby.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldier ants are a caste of ant, so the colony's mound is whimsically their barracks, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Cuddle when model visits is exactly what's needed

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone's place, so one piece enters another

parts.note: to spoon is to cuddle lying curled together
the Model T was Ford's famous early car

explanation.surface: A hug when a fashion model drops by is just the thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' suggests a fashion model, but it is the Ford car's letter, placed in the middle of the cuddling verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means completely accurate or perfectly right, so it describes precisely the thing required.

clue.text: One might take issue if head chases child

indicators.note: one who chases comes behind, so this piece follows the other in order

parts.note: a kid is a child
napper is old British slang for the head

explanation.surface: Someone might object if a headteacher runs after a pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take issue' means object in the surface; read literally, issue is offspring, and one who takes children is an abductor.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue means children, so someone who seizes a child and holds them is literally taking issue.

clue.text: See German film about heads of the IMF

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for German

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: E.T. is Spielberg's 1982 film about an alien

indicators.note: the head of anything is its top, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: the opening letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Watch a German movie about the bosses of the International Monetary Fund.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like an instruction to watch the film, but it is the definition, as in 'I see'.
explanation.definitionFit: To see a point is to understand it, and the idiom is the colloquial way of saying you have understood.

clue.text: Indian thrones seen in building a disappointment

indicators.note: what is seen in something is visible within it, so the letters sit inside the words

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word, the article and the start of the last

explanation.surface: An Indian palace built with regal thrones turns out a letdown.
explanation.walkthrough: A gadi (or gaddi) is the cushioned throne of an Indian ruler; the plural is spelled across three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Gadi is a Hindi word for a royal seat or cushioned throne of an Indian prince.

clue.text: Some stoners or goths will score grass

indicators.note: some means a portion of the whole, so a piece of the words makes the answer

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Some potheads or goths will buy marijuana.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Score grass' sounds like buying cannabis, but grass is the definition, a sweet sorghum.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorgo is sweet sorghum, a cereal plant of the grass family grown for syrup and fodder.

clue.text: Drill mate sorted out for gym equipment

indicators.note: sorting out a jumble puts things in fresh order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An exercise partner is organised so the workout kit gets used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drill' fits the gym picture as an exercise routine, but it and the partner are only letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadmill is a machine with a moving belt for running or walking indoors, a staple of any fitness centre.

clue.text: Voucher in court bitten by racoon in America

indicators.note: something bitten is held between the jaws, so one piece is gripped inside another

parts.note: coon is an American colloquial shortening for the racoon
to be up before a judge is to be in court

explanation.surface: A voucher produced in court is chewed by a raccoon in the USA.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In court' looks like a location, but the phrase 'up before the magistrates' supplies the inner piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A coupon is a slip entitling the holder to a discount or goods, the same as a voucher.

clue.text: When to probe new friend in a nosey way?

indicators.note: a probe is pushed inside something, so one piece goes within the others

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: A question about when to pry into a new friend's life, nosily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nosey' suggests prying, but the question mark signals the literal sense: of or through the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Nasally means through the nose, so the whimsical 'nosey' here means relating to the nose rather than inquisitive.
